title: Why is the general recommendation "use coalesce to reduce partitions, repartition to increase" — and what is the performance trade-off of `repartition(1)` vs `coalesce(1)` (repartition shuffles all data to one partition; coalesce stitches but may create a single large task)?
shortTitle: Why "coalesce to reduce, repartition to increase" — and the `repartition(1)` vs `coalesce(1)` trade-off

s1_definition.profdef: The guideline "coalesce to reduce, repartition to increase" follows from how each operation works. Coalesce is a narrow transformation that merges existing partitions without a shuffle, so it is cheap but can only reduce the count. Repartition is a wide transformation that performs a full shuffle, so it can both increase and decrease the count and always produces balanced partitions. For a simple reduction you prefer coalesce because it avoids network cost; to increase parallelism or force even sizes you must use repartition because only a shuffle can create new, balanced partitions.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, reducing the number of clerks handling slips is like merging two neighbouring stacks — no slip has to walk across the room, so you just coalesce. But increasing the number of clerks means some slips genuinely have to move to new desks, and you cannot create new desks without moving slips, so you must repartition. Collapsing everything to one clerk is a special case: coalesce makes that one clerk also do all the upstream sorting alone, while repartition first redistributes then collapses — different costs, same final single stack.
s1_definition.oneliner: Coalesce merges cheaply but only shrinks; repartition shuffles to both grow and balance — so reduce with coalesce, increase with repartition.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The guideline "coalesce to reduce, repartition to increase" follows from how each operation works. Coalesce is a narrow transformation that merges existing partitions without a shuffle, so it is cheap but can only reduce the count. Repartition is a wide transformation that performs a full shuffle, so it can both increase and decrease the count and always produces balanced partitions. For a simple reduction you prefer coalesce because it avoids network cost; to increase parallelism or force even sizes you must use repartition because only a shuffle can create new, balanced partitions.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, reducing the number of clerks handling slips is like merging two neighbouring stacks — no slip has to walk across the room, so you just coalesce. But increasing the number of clerks means some slips genuinely have to move to new desks, and you cannot create new desks without moving slips, so you must repartition. Collapsing everything to one clerk is a special case: coalesce makes that one clerk also do all the upstream sorting alone, while repartition first redistributes then collapses — different costs, same final single stack.

**One line to remember:** Coalesce merges cheaply but only shrinks; repartition shuffles to both grow and balance — so reduce with coalesce, increase with repartition.

sections.s2_technical:
Coalesce when reducing is cheap because of its narrow dependency: several parent partitions feed one child on the same executor, so no data crosses the network. But this same narrowness means it cannot increase the count — you cannot split one partition into two without moving data, and coalesce refuses to move data. If you ask coalesce for more partitions than you have, it quietly does nothing. That is why "increase" always means repartition.

Repartition always shuffles. For increasing, the shuffle is unavoidable: creating more partitions requires redistributing records. For reducing, repartition still shuffles, which is more expensive than coalesce, but it buys you perfectly even partitions. So the recommendation is really about cost: if you are reducing and do not need perfect balance, coalesce saves the shuffle; if you are increasing or you need balance, repartition is the only tool.

The `repartition(1)` versus `coalesce(1)` comparison is the sharpest illustration. Both end with a single partition holding all the data, but the path differs. `coalesce(1)` is narrow, so there is no shuffle boundary — the single final task also runs every upstream transformation in the same chain, which means all the preceding work is squeezed into one task with no parallelism at all. That can be catastrophic if the upstream work is heavy. `repartition(1)` inserts a shuffle: the upstream transformations run with full parallelism across many tasks, each writes its shuffle output, and then a single reduce task gathers everything into one partition. You pay for the shuffle, but the expensive upstream work stays parallel.

A senior-level nuance: neither single-partition option is good for large data, because one partition means one task holds everything, risking out-of-memory. For writing a single file over large data, the better pattern is to keep parallelism and let the file system or a downstream step merge, or to accept multiple files. `repartition(1)` is the lesser evil when upstream work is heavy; `coalesce(1)` is acceptable only when the dataset is already small and upstream work is trivial.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A regulatory report at the National Bank of India must be delivered as one CSV file. The job computes the report with an expensive aggregation across 200 partitions, then needs a single output. An engineer writes `coalesce(1)`. Because coalesce has no shuffle boundary, the expensive aggregation is forced into a single task and the job runs for hours. This is exactly the `coalesce(1)` trap — the single final partition drags the whole upstream chain into one task.

Problem 2 — The fix is `repartition(1)`: the aggregation runs across 200 tasks in parallel, then a shuffle gathers the results into one final partition for the single file. It costs a shuffle but keeps the heavy work parallel.

Problem 3 — Separately, after a light filter the data sits in 200 tiny partitions and must shrink to 10 files. Here coalesce is correct: it merges cheaply with no shuffle because there is no heavy upstream work to serialize.

The demo models a pipeline's effective upstream parallelism and estimated cost for coalesce(1), repartition(1), and coalesce(10) after a light filter, showing when each is right.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/spark-partition-advisor-1.0.0.jar com.bank.spark.PartitionAdvisorDemo

# In a real Spark job:
#   df.coalesce(10)       # reduce cheaply after a light filter
#   df.repartition(64)    # increase parallelism (shuffle required)
#   df.repartition(1)     # one file, heavy upstream: keeps upstream parallel
#   df.coalesce(1)        # one file, ONLY if upstream work is trivial
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three partitioning decisions — a one-file regulatory report with heavy upstream work, a shrink to ten after a light filter, and an increase from eight to sixty-four before a join.

Step 1: For the one-file report, the advisor sees the target is one and upstream work is heavy. It recommends `repartition(1)` and notes that upstream parallelism of 200 is preserved because the inserted shuffle decouples the heavy aggregation from the single final partition.

Step 2: For the shrink after a light filter, the advisor sees the target is ten and upstream work is light, so a shuffle buys nothing. It recommends `coalesce(10)`, a cheap narrow merge.

Step 3: For the increase from eight to sixty-four, the advisor knows new partitions cannot be created without moving data, so it recommends `repartition(64)`.

Step 4: The demo logs each recommendation with its reasoning and warns against the coalesce-to-one trap when upstream work is heavy.

Final output:


sections.s6_takeaway:
The recommendation to coalesce when reducing and repartition when increasing comes straight from the mechanics. Coalesce is a narrow transformation that merges existing partitions on the same executor without any network movement, so it is cheap but can only reduce the count — you cannot create new partitions without moving data, and coalesce refuses to move data. Repartition is a wide transformation that performs a full shuffle, so it can both increase and decrease and it always produces balanced partitions. Therefore, for a plain reduction where perfect balance does not matter, coalesce saves the shuffle; to increase parallelism or to force even sizes, repartition is the only option.

The clearest illustration is one partition. Both coalesce of one and repartition of one end with all data in a single partition, but the path is completely different. Coalesce of one is narrow, so there is no shuffle boundary, and the single final task is forced to also run every upstream transformation — all the heavy work is squeezed into one task with no parallelism. Repartition of one inserts a shuffle, so the upstream work runs in parallel across many tasks and only the final gather into one partition is single-threaded. You pay for the shuffle, but you keep the expensive work parallel.

In my work at the National Bank of India I saw a regulatory report that had to be a single CSV written with coalesce of one, and because the aggregation upstream was heavy, the whole job was serialized into one task and ran for hours. Switching to repartition of one kept the aggregation parallel across two hundred tasks and only gathered at the end, and the runtime dropped dramatically. Conversely, when I only needed to shrink many tiny partitions after a light filter, coalesce was correct because there was no heavy upstream work to serialize. So my rule in interviews is: reduce with coalesce, increase with repartition, and when collapsing to a single partition over heavy work, prefer repartition of one because coalesce of one drags the entire upstream chain into one task.
